_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Mathematics unit lecture film, Lesson 2 Patterns and Square Numbers. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the lesson page's own teaching slides in order - pairing counters off (slide 2), what adding and taking away do to odd and even (slides 2 and 3), a shape for an unknown quantity in an addition (slide 6) and then with the shape first in a take-away (slide 7), linear and non-linear sequences named as the lesson names them, with their term-to-term rule (slides 9-10), the spatial pattern of square numbers (slide 11) and the L between one square and the next (slide 12) - and uses the lesson's own numbers throughout: 8 and 7, 7 + 5 = 12, 9 - 3 = 6, 15 + triangle = 22, triangle take away 14 = 30, so triangle = 44 (slide 7's own example), 5 12 19 26 linear, 2 5 9 14 non-linear, 4 by 4 = 16, and 6 by 6 growing into 7 by 7 with an L of 13.
title: Patterns and Square Numbers
subtitle: Grade 4 Mathematics
objectives: Recognise and explain generalisations when adding and subtracting combinations of even and odd numbers.
Recognise the use of objects, shapes or symbols to represent unknown quantities in addition and subtraction calculations.
Recognise and extend linear and non-linear sequences, and describe the term-to- term rule.
Recognise and extend the spatial pattern of square numbers.

beats.say: Some numbers pair off exactly. Others always leave one over.
And some numbers make a perfect square of dots, like 16.
Take some counters and pair them off, two by two.
8 makes four whole pairs, and nothing is left over. So 8 is even.
Now try 7. It makes three pairs and one left over, so 7 is odd.
That one left over is the whole story. Watch what it does next.
Add 7 and 5. Both are odd, so each one has a leftover.
Put them together. The two leftovers find each other and make a pair.
So 7 add 5 is 12, and 12 is even. Two odd numbers make an even one.

at.rule: Two odd numbers make an even one

beats.say: Taking away follows the same rule. 9 take away 3 leaves 6.
Both leftovers cancel, so 6 pairs up exactly. It is even too.

scenes.heading: The shape that hides a number

beats.say: A shape in a sum stands for a number nobody has told you yet.

at.number: a number nobody has told you yet

beats.say: 15 add triangle is 22. The triangle has to fill the gap.
22 take away 15 is 7, so the triangle must be 7. It is not a guess.
Sometimes the shape comes first, in a take-away: triangle take away 14 is 30.
Put the two parts back together: 30 add 14 is 44. The triangle is 44.

at.together: Put the two parts back together

beats.say: A sequence follows a rule from one term to the next one.

at.next: from one term to the next one

beats.say: Look at 5, 12, 19, 26. Take each term away from the one after it.
Every step is add 7, the same each time. That makes it linear, and the next term is 33.
Now look at 2, 5, 9, 14. The steps are add 3, then add 4, then add 5.
Those steps change every time, so it is non-linear. The rule is to add one more than before.
A square number is one you can lay out as a perfect square of dots.
Here are 4 rows of 4 dots. Count them: that is 16 altogether.
So 16 is a square number. We write it as 4 squared.
It means a number times itself: 4 times 4 is 16, not 8.
The first four square numbers are 1, 4, 9 and 16. Look at them grow.

scenes.heading: Between one square and the next

beats.say: To grow a square by one, you add a whole L along two edges.

at.ell: a whole L along two edges

beats.say: A 6 by 6 square needs 6 new dots down the side and 6 along the bottom.
And one more in the corner, where the two arms meet. That makes 13.
6 times 6 is 36, and 7 times 7 is 49. The gap is 13, just as we counted.
Every L is the next odd number: 3, then 5, then 7, then 9.
Even numbers pair off exactly. Odd numbers always leave one over.

at.odd: Odd numbers always leave one over

beats.say: Two odd numbers, added or taken away, give you an even one.
A shape hides a number, and a sequence follows a rule you can say.
And a square number really does make a square of dots. Go and build one.
